title: OpenAI Fired 3 Safety Researchers Over Disappearing Signal Chats With External Researcher
summary:
Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang were dismissed from OpenAI last month after security staff discovered disappearing messages on their personal Signal accounts. The firings followed a leak investigation into a story published by The Information about the proprietary designs of OpenAI's Astra model and its use of opaque architectures.

OpenAI suspected the researchers of sharing secret model designs with outside expert Ryan Greenblatt, who denied facilitating any leaks. While an OpenAI spokeswoman said the use of the Signal app was not approved, the company stated that such usage was not the only reason for the dismissals. The three researchers had spent the preceding months pushing the company to keep AI chain-of-thought processes visible to humans.

Part of me refuses to believe OpenAI fired three safety researchers for political reasons, and wishes instead that it was just a badly executed investigation mixed with paranoia and lack of sleep after a rollercoaster summer. 

But given that OpenAI continues to not be able to say anything that makes sense to me about our firings and keeps acting adversarially (e.g. claiming to journalists I wasn't on the Hugging Face investigation, while there're a number of people who could confirm otherwise), it's hard to not become cynical.

selectedTweets.bestBit: OpenAI then fired three safety researchers for having disappearing messages on Signal chats on their personal phone with Greenblatt.
selectedTweets.text:
Wow. Per this reporting:

- OpenAI investigators decided that Ryan Greenblatt had been the source for The Information story on a new technique improving capabilities at the expense of monitorability (recurrent depth i.e. quasi-neuralese)
- OpenAI then fired three safety researchers for having disappearing messages on Signal chats on their personal phone with Greenblatt.

Greenblatt denies that he was the source for the story, telling the Journal “I take confidentiality very seriously and never share such information with reporters." FWIW, I think there are number of reasons to believe him:

- Safety researchers are often the most skittish about leaking to journos fearing that getting caught would blow back on safety writ large. This dynamic is even more pronounced for safety researchers at third parties, whose access is wholly determined by the company.
- If he wanted to sound the alarm about this technique, he wouldn't have leaked to a publication with a famously expensive and insurmountable paywall (which, btw, has probably the best sourcing at AI cos).
- I've interviewed him and separately chatted with him a few times over the years, and IMO he's too rationalist to lie directly.
- OpenAI provided no evidence to the WSJ that Greenblatt was involved.

OpenAI tells the Journal that the firings were for more than just the Signal chats, but doesn't substantiate. Disappearing messages on Signal, as the piece mentions, are indeed a common practice in Silicon Valley.

Regardless of the underlying facts of the case, it's clear that the way OpenAI has handled this has had a chilling effect on employee conduct. Each of the three fired researchers publicly criticized the company in the weeks leading up to the firings. I haven't seen that kind of public criticism from employees since (though I'm told there's pushback happening internally in Slack). People have understandably gotten more skittish about talking to me as well. If OpenAI were actually trying to avoid chilling employee speech, the company would share a lot more information than they have.

selectedTweets.text:
It is striking the extent to which after reading this WSJ article - an article that OpenAI commented on repeatedly and from three reporters who are deeply sourced within OpenAI - I still don't really know what evidence OpenAI has that merited these firings.

Put yourself in the shoes of an employee working on AI safety at OpenAI. 

After reading this article would you have a clear sense of what lines these employees crossed that merited their firing? 

Or not knowing the exact lines, would you generally pull back from interactions with third parties that could later be cited as evidence of disloyalty?

OpenAI’s reasons for firing them are no clearer after this article than they were at 2pm on the day it fired them. But the issues they were raising are more important than ever. Proud @psst_org has been able to support them.
